prize_parts.citation: For a visionary body of prose, rooted in lyric poetry, that builds memory, the body and dream into a patterned metaphysical cosmos of exceptional imaginative and formal ambition.

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged in laureate and prize part: B043, Mircea Cărtărescu as the single credited writer. The citation is changed. In round 1 I wrote 'prose and poetry' as if they were co-equal. Round 1 showed that the translated evidence for the poetry and essays is thinner than for the novels. I now make the prose carry the citation and name poetry only as its root. I also drop any wording that claims lineage, completeness or 'a lifetime's work', because none of us can argue those from the texts. The merit case rests on the criteria. The voice is distinctive: from public descriptions of the Orbitor/Blinding trilogy and Solenoid, dense, recursive prose turns body, memory and dream into one structure. The formal ambition is real, since these books renew what a novel can hold. Public accounts also describe a project that runs from the early shorter fiction and verse through the trilogy to the later novel. That fits the idea, which I took from my own Academy reading, that what is judged is a whole authorship and not one title. The sources are public accounts, and I have not verified the texts. The fact that all six first-round files name the same writer is not an argument, and I do not use it as one. The case holds only if the voice and structure survive scrutiny of the books, and I have tried to test that against the strongest alternatives.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is unchanged. The effect depends on the density and rhythm of Romanian prose, which I can assess only through translation and critical description. The chair's questions sharpen the real risk, which is that the digressive, maximalist mode reads as excess in the longest books. Then 'sustained ambition' would not amount to 'sustained quality', and the breadth of significance would be narrower than the scale suggests. My own breadth worry is not fully answered. Colleagues point to range across bodily, historical, comic and speculative material and across verse and prose, but they hold that with caution too, and so do I. Nobody on the committee has named which volumes beyond Blinding and Solenoid best show sustained quality. I would lower B043 if readers of the later books or original-language critics reported that the late novels repeat the earlier project, or that the shorter fiction and verse do not show the range claimed. I would then move to Adonis, whose formal case is the most secure of the alternatives on breadth of influence, although my access to it is also limited.

responses.point: Olsson moved Cărtărescu from second to first. He keeps Carson as first alternative, though he places less weight on her modest corpus. He argues that her translations and scholarship are part of one sustained engagement with antiquity that feeds her original work, and he calls the fit with the will's wording a legitimate dispute.
responses.response: I value the reasons Olsson gives for his revision. He moved because of questions about sustained significance, not because of how many colleagues ranked Cărtărescu, and that is the standard I want to apply too. His point that Carson's translations feed her original work is coherent, and it moves me a little. I now see the translations as a possible source of the work's depth, and no longer as only a complication in separating the oeuvre. I do not think it removes the problem I raised in round 1. A whole-oeuvre citation has to rest on a body of original achievement, and I cannot tell from public knowledge whether that body is larger than Autobiography of Red and Nox. Olsson says the will's wording is disputable and does not resolve it, and I agree it is unresolved. I do not exclude hybrid work by category, but I also cannot say her work meets the will's standard. If a member with more classical grounding could show a developing arc in the original work, I would reconsider Carson, but not enough to move her above B043.

responses.point: Mattson says the full oeuvre, including poetry and shorter prose, must be the basis of judgment. She argues the project moves between bodily, autobiographical, grotesque, comic and speculative registers, but holds this with caution. She would build the citation mainly on the prose and mention poetry only if the committee can read enough of it.
responses.response: Her proposal to build the citation mainly on the prose is the one I have adopted. My revised wording follows it. On breadth, her list of registers is the best answer so far to my worry that the inward mode narrows the significance. It is an answer from public description, and I have not verified it. I still think it is a different claim from showing significance beyond the work's own interior. The test I would apply is whether the comic and grotesque registers and the shorter fiction do real work in the project, or only decorate a single mode. If they do, my breadth concern largely goes. I also agree with her on Michon: his formal rigor is not in doubt, and our difference concerns how much a small corpus can show about sustained range and how much translation can carry of a style that lives in syntax and register.

responses.point: Carlberg asks whether Palm's lower placement of Adonis is a judgment about the poetry or about how much translation can carry. She argues that if it is the second, the limit applies to every language-bound candidate, Cărtărescu included, and so should not be applied selectively.
responses.response: The symmetry point is correct, and it applies to my own ordering as well. My doubts about judging Adonis's prosody directly are the same kind of doubts I have about Cărtărescu's Romanian sentences. The difference is one of degree. For a novelist's large structures, such as recurrence, scale and the movement between registers, translation preserves more than it does for the sound of Arabic verse. I do not treat that as a decisive difference, though, and it does not entitle me to rank Adonis lower on a quality judgment. It only entitles me to say that my confidence is lower. That is why he stays as my first alternative and not my first choice. I would be uncomfortable if the committee treated the limits of its reading as a settled verdict on either writer. If original-language readers could testify on the Arabic poetry and on the Romanian prose, that would improve the judgment more than any further argument among those of us who read both in translation.

responses.point: Palm separates sustained ambition from sustained quality. She says the claim that the later novels extend and do not repeat the earlier ones comes from public knowledge, and she would reconsider Carson if a developing arc in her later work could be shown.
responses.response: That distinction is the most useful one in round 1, and my uncertainty is organized around it. On the question of extending or repeating, the supplied evidence gives us only public accounts, and I cannot add direct reading of the late books. The question for my vote is whether Solenoid carries on the project of the trilogy in a new direction, or restates it at similar scale. Public descriptions suggest the former, but a committee should not take a reputation as proof of sustained quality. I would also back Palm's openness on Carson: it is the right standard, and it is the same standard I apply to Cărtărescu. A claim of development needs specific works, not a general assertion, and no member has yet named those works for either writer.

uncertainties: How much of Cărtărescu's stylistic achievement survives translation is unresolved. My assessment rests on public knowledge and critical description, not on independent verification of the texts or reading in Romanian.
Whether the late novels extend the project or repeat it, and whether the digressive density is depth or excess in the longest books, are not settled by the supplied evidence.
The poetry and essays are thinner in translation than the novels, so the whole-oeuvre judgment is partial, and the citation therefore rests on the prose.
Whether the inward, maximalist mode has the breadth of significance claimed is a disagreement among members, and the answers offered rest on public descriptions only.
Adonis's prosodic and linguistic achievement cannot be judged directly in translation, and whether his late work sustains the earlier level is unclear to me.

How the committee should weigh Anne Carson's translations, adaptations and book-object works as original literary achievement is unresolved, as is whether her hybrid mode is central or specialized. My low placement of her reflects my limited ability to judge that, not a settled verdict.

In round 1 I named the subject of Alexis Wright's collective memoir as Tracker Wilson. Carlberg gives Tracker Tilmouth, which is closer to my recollection of public knowledge. I withdraw my version as likely an error, but I have not verified either name, and it does not affect my ranking.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile, which records committee service with the other five members but no personal, professional or family connection to any shortlisted writer. My own practice as a novelist and my earlier stated interest in women writers and a global reading of literature are general context, not evidence of a preference for any shortlisted candidate. Conflicts are disclosed here and not adjudicated.
